prose_changes.old: The World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh in 1910 set three streams running: the International Missionary Council, founded in 1921; Life and Work, from 1925; and Faith and Order, from 1927. These converged into the World Council of Churches, constituted at Amsterdam in 1948, with the missionary council merging in at New Delhi in 1961. Orthodox churches were members, while the Roman Catholic Church worked alongside it without joining. It stands as a counterpart to the Lausanne movement of 1974, the evangelical alternative answer to the same question of how divided churches should work together, and it grew out of the institutional world built by mainline liberal Protestantism and neo-orthodoxy. In Africa, churches formed the All Africa Conference of Churches. It was founded at its first assembly in Kampala on 20 April 1963, after a conference at Ibadan in 1958. In 1971 the Kenyan theologian John Gatu first called for a moratorium on missionaries. The conference's third assembly met at Lusaka in May 1974.
prose_changes.new: The World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh in 1910 set three streams running. The International Missionary Council began in 1921, Life and Work in 1925, and Faith and Order in 1927. These came together in the World Council of Churches, formed at Amsterdam in 1948. The missionary council joined it at New Delhi in 1961. Orthodox churches were members. In 1920 the Ecumenical Patriarchate had called for a fellowship of churches. The Roman Catholic Church did not join. In 1928 Pope Pius XI ruled that Catholics could not take part. After the Second Vatican Council, Rome worked with it. In its first years most of its member churches were Protestant and Western. It may have grown in part out of the world of the mainline churches, but the evidence for that is thin. This map sets it beside the Lausanne movement of 1974, an evangelical answer to the same question: how should divided churches work together? prose_changes.old: The World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh in 1910 left three currents running, which came together over the following decades. The International Missionary Council was founded in October 1921; Life and Work, concerned with the churches' common action in society, took shape in 1925; Faith and Order, concerned with the doctrinal questions that divided them, in 1927. The last two merged into the World Council of Churches, constituted at Amsterdam on 22 August 1948 with 147 member churches, and the International Missionary Council joined them at New Delhi in 1961. It was a council of churches, not a church. It had no authority over its members and no confession of its own, and each member body kept its own. Orthodox churches were members. The Roman Catholic Church was not, and worked with it in other ways. In the Middle East, the Middle East Council of Churches held its first assembly at Nicosia from 28 to 30 May 1974.

prose_changes.old: In 2010 it was a living institution, and it had been the century's principal experiment in getting separated churches to act and argue together in one room. Its assemblies and its Faith and Order work produced a large body of shared statements on questions that had divided churches for centuries, and its member churches used them. This map draws it as the counter-pole to the Lausanne movement of 1974 — two different answers, from the same century, to the question of how churches that disagree should work together — and as the institutional home of the mainline century that built it.

This map draws it as the counter-pole to the Lausanne movement of 1974. They are two answers, from the same century, to one question: how should churches that disagree work together? prose_changes.old: The movement itself ended. Rauschenbusch died in 1918, and the war took the confidence out of a theology built on the expectation that the kingdom was arriving through reform; Reinhold Niebuhr's Moral Man and Immoral Society (1932) later made the criticism stick. But the stream did not stop — it was absorbed into the mainline denominations' own social agencies, and the mainline century that follows on this map is its named heir. The Social Creed of 1908 stands behind the denominational social statements that followed it. And In His Steps left something odder and more durable: the question 'what would Jesus do' was still in circulation a hundred years after the novel that put it there.

Janani Luwum is commemorated among the twentieth-century martyrs on the west front of Westminster Abbey, unveiled in 1998.

prose_changes.old: In 1982 John Wimber and C. Peter Wagner began teaching MC510, 'Signs and Wonders', at Fuller Theological Seminary in Pasadena. The course ran until 1985 and drew controversy. Fuller's faculty dropped it in early 1986 and published its own study, Ministry and the Miraculous, in 1987. Wagner called the stream 'the Third Wave'. Its people believed in the power and gifts of the Holy Spirit. Yet they did not adopt Pentecostal or charismatic theology or worship styles. Wimber set out his method in Power Evangelism in 1985. In 1994 a revival called the Toronto Blessing began at the Toronto Airport Vineyard. The Vineyard association cut its ties with that church in December 1995. Margaret Poloma published a study of the revival in 1997. Jon Bialecki later studied 'the Third Wave' by name, and the Vineyard as 'an American charismatic movement'.

Two judgment calls for the reviewer, not escalations: the major test on Mortalium Animos (a papal encyclical laying down a rule for all Catholics, judged 'council-law') and on Bishop Stuart's 1943 'New Way' (one bishop's settlement, judged 'rule-changed').

Not an escalation, but worth Mark's eye: the ecumenical movement's entry said it 'grew out of the institutional world built by mainline liberal Protestantism and neo-orthodoxy' and called the mainline 'the century that built it'. The council's own history names student movements, Edinburgh 1910 and the 1920 Orthodox encyclical as its roots, and says it was Protestant and Western at first. The fix fits in a clause ('may have grown in part out of'), so it is a prose change, not a rewrite.
